content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is defined as heavy bleeding occurring within the first 24 hours after childbirth and is a leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. Antifibrinolytic drugs, particularly tranexamic acid (TXA), have demonstrated efficacy in reducing bleeding during surgical procedures and in trauma patients, where they have been shown to lower mortality rates without increasing the risk of adverse events. This review focuses specifically on the use of antifibrinolytic drugs for the treatment of primary PPH, as opposed to previous reviews that examined a broader range of treatments. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of antifibrinolytic drugs, such as TXA, aprotinin, epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA), and aminomethylbenzoic acid, in the treatment of primary PPH. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women diagnosed with PPH after a pregnancy of at least 24 weeks' gestation, regardless of the mode of delivery (vaginal or cesarean). However, only studies investigating TXA were identified, and no trials on EACA, aprotinin, or aminomethylbenzoic acid were found. Three trials involving a total of 20,412 women met the inclusion criteria. Two large trials (20,212 women) compared intravenous (IV) TXA with placebo or standard care in hospital settings across high-, middle-, and low-income countries. The largest of these, the WOMAN trial, contributed over 99% of the data and was assessed as having a low risk of bias. A smaller trial conducted in Iran compared IV TXA with rectal misoprostol but did not report on the primary outcomes of this review. The evidence from these trials indicates that IV TXA reduces the risk of maternal death due to bleeding, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65 to 1.00; moderate-quality evidence). The effect was most pronounced when TXA was administered within one to three hours after childbirth (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.88), with no apparent benefit when given after three hours. There was no significant difference in the effect of TXA based on the mode of delivery. Fewer deaths from all causes were observed in women receiving TXA, although the confidence interval crossed the line of no effect (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.05; moderate-quality evidence). One trial with 151 women suggested that TXA may reduce the likelihood of blood loss of ≥500 mL after randomization (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.93; low-quality evidence). However, TXA did not significantly reduce the risk of serious maternal morbidity (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.19; high-quality evidence), hysterectomy to control bleeding (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.12; high-quality evidence), or the need for blood transfusion (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.03; moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, there was no significant reduction in maternal vascular occlusive events, although the results for this outcome were imprecise (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.43; moderate-quality evidence). Interestingly, the use of TXA was associated with an increased use of brace sutures (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.41) and a decreased need for laparotomy to control bleeding (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.85). In conclusion, IV TXA reduces mortality due to bleeding in women with primary PPH without increasing the risk of thromboembolic events. The evidence supports the early administration of TXA, ideally within three hours of childbirth, to maximize its effectiveness. However, in non-hospital settings where IV administration may not be feasible, alternative routes of administration should be explored to ensure broader accessibility to this life-saving treatment.
